item.title: China-initiated Luban Workshops empower global youth with practical skills
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 08:09:00
Participants view exhibits at an exhibition during the World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference 2026 in Tianjin, north China, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Ran) At an automotive industrial park in north China's Tianjin Municipality, Egyptian students Abdelrahman Ayman Zaky and Adham Ayman are gaining hands-on experience in new energy vehicle (NEV) chassis systems alongside their Chinese peers. Having acquired vocational skills at an Egyptian Luban Workshop, the two came to China to deepen their expertise. Adham, 20, hopes to improve his Chinese and vehicle maintenance skills before returning to Egypt to pursue a career as an automotive engineer. Their experience highlights the mission of the China-initiated Luban Workshops, which over the past decade have equipped young people worldwide with useful skills, fostered local talent, and supported industrial development. Named after Luban, an ancient Chinese craftsman and inventor who lived more than 2,500 years ago, the initiative draws on a longstanding Chinese tradition of craftsmanship and innovation. Jointly established by Chinese and foreign educational institutions, Luban Workshops now offer vocational education and skills-training programs in 32 countries. In Egypt, Luban Workshops are helping students like Adham translate classroom learning into engineering capabilities. Mohamed Mostafa, a student at an Egyptian Luban Workshop now studying at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said hands-on practice has strengthened his ability to tackle real-world engineering challenges. "In the EPIP (Engineering Practice and Innovation Project) classroom, we don't just work on simulated problems. We work on real-world engineering problems in teams, discussing solutions, refining our techniques and testing them again and again. We break down complex challenges to achieve the best results and meet engineering standards," Mostafa said. He added that he has shared the approach with students in Egypt, where they have applied the same methods to develop their own projects. The two Egyptian Luban Workshops have provided formal education to more than 3,100 people and skills training on over 4,000 occasions, creating new opportunities for industrial cooperation. Wang Baolong, dean of the School of Mechanical Engineering at Tianjin Light Industry Vocational Technical College, said graduates trained in advanced technologies can meet the needs of local businesses, strengthening Chinese companies' confidence in investing in and establishing factories in Egypt while supporting local economic development. An employment training base jointly established by the Egyptian Luban Workshops and the China-Egypt TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone has provided young Egyptians with a direct pathway to employment. "After receiving professional technical training, these young people can operate production equipment proficiently. They are exactly the kind of skilled workers that companies need," Wang added. Beyond teaching technical skills, the workshops also help build local capacity for sustained vocational training. While setting up training centers and supplying advanced equipment, Chinese partners send teachers and technicians to train local instructors and arrange exchanges and learning opportunities in China. In 2016, the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College and the Ayutthaya Technical College in Thailand jointly established the world's first Luban Workshop. Over the past decade, all six of the workshop's internationalized majors have been incorporated into Thailand's national education system. "We are not just cultivating talent for the local area, but leaving the whole system behind. Chinese standards and models are truly integrating into and promoting local development," said Mei Wentao, a staff member at the Tianjin Bohai Vocational Technical College. More than 100 Chinese companies in Thailand operate businesses ranging from NEV components to vehicle distribution. In August 2025, the China-Thailand automotive intelligent manufacturing industry-education integration community was established in Thailand. With a steady supply of skilled graduates, companies can recruit directly from schools, helping young Thai people find jobs more easily and quickly. In Central Asia, the Tajik Luban Workshop is helping local young people explore new career opportunities. In nearly four years of operation, it has provided learning and training opportunities to more than 3,600 undergraduate and postgraduate students. When Bakhtiyor Bozorzoda enrolled at the Tajik Technical University, he was uncertain about his chosen major in geodesy and cartography. Advanced surveying equipment, digital mapping technologies, and virtual simulation courses at the Tajik Luban Workshop helped him recognize the field's potential and develop a stronger interest in surveying. During his studies, Bozorzoda gained hands-on experience with high-precision instruments and digital mapping technologies. "I hope to continue my studies in China in the future, learn more advanced surveying technologies and contribute to infrastructure development in Tajikistan," he said. Today, Luban Workshops have become a hallmark of China's international vocational education cooperation. Data from China's Ministry of Education show that the country has established 38 Luban Workshops in 32 countries, providing formal education to more than 30,000 students and non-degree training to over 160,000 people. The Luban Workshops reflect a commitment to harmony, coexistence and the common good in Chinese cultural tradition. By responding to local needs, they help young people in different countries acquire skills that can benefit them throughout their careers, said Tian Xuejun, president of the China Education Association for International Exchange, at the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, held in Tianjin from Oct. 15 to 17. China has the world's largest vocational education system, with 9,151 secondary vocational schools, 1,554 higher vocational colleges and 124 vocational undergraduate institutions. As of the end of 2025, China's vocational education catalog covered 19 major categories, 97 subcategories and 1,491 majors, spanning virtually all sectors of the national economy and all 41 major industrial categories. China is continuing to strengthen its vocational education system to support the development of emerging industries and expand opportunities for people both at home and abroad. At the 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, representatives from 45 countries jointly released the Framework of World Vocational and Technical Education Standards developed under China's leadership. The framework calls for improving vocational school systems, establishing lifelong education and training opportunities for all, developing teaching materials through industry-education collaboration, building teaching teams through school-enterprise partnerships, and using artificial intelligence to drive reform in education and teaching.

item.title: China makes significant progress in climate action, charts green path
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-22 07:51:00
An aerial drone photo taken on July 16, 2024 shows a solar thermal energy storage power station in Guazhou County, northwest China's Gansu Province. (Xinhua) China has achieved significant results in tackling climate change in recent years, gradually forging a green and low-carbon development path, a senior environment official said on Wednesday. Li Gao, vice minister of ecology and environment, made the remarks at a news conference, where an annual report on China's policies and actions on climate change was released by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment. The report showed that in 2025, China's carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP fell by 17.7 percent compared with 2020 levels. Non-fossil energy accounted for 21.7 percent of total energy consumption last year, while combined installed capacity of wind and solar power reached 1.84 billion kilowatts. Forest stock volume stood at 20.99 billion cubic meters in 2025. This progress is backed by the country's sustained efforts to accelerate its green and low-carbon transformation. China has built the world's largest and most complete clean energy industrial chain, with green and low-carbon industries becoming an important engine of economic growth, Li said. By mid-2026, the country's total installed renewable energy capacity had reached 2.46 billion kilowatts, accounting for 60.7 percent of total national power generation capacity. At the end of July, installed solar power capacity had surpassed coal power for the first time in China's history, making it the country's largest single power source. Moreover, China's combined installed capacity of operational and approved nuclear power units has risen to first place globally. New energy vehicle production and sales, meanwhile, have ranked first in the world for 11 consecutive years. Li noted that the country has established the world's largest carbon emission trading market, covering about 8.3 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide, or more than 65 percent of the country's total emissions. Cumulative allowance trading volume recently surpassed 1 billion tonnes. China has long placed high importance on addressing climate change. It has set the dual carbon goals of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060. China last year announced its 2035 nationally determined contributions, including a target of reducing economy-wide net greenhouse gas emissions by 7 percent to 10 percent from peak levels, while striving to do better. It represented the first time China had put forward an absolute emission reduction target covering all greenhouse gases across the entire economy, Li said. The country is also actively participating in and leading global climate governance while helping other developing countries build their capacity to address climate change. China has signed South-South cooperation memoranda of understanding on climate change with 46 developing countries, helped build low-carbon demonstration zones, implemented a series of flagship climate projects, and trained more than 10,000 officials and technical personnel from over 120 developing countries. China in 2023 launched the "Africa Solar Belt" photovoltaic project, which has helped nearly 20,000 households in five African countries gain access to electricity and lighting. By 2027, this flagship project is expected to benefit 50,000 African households. Looking ahead, China's commitment to addressing climate change will not waver. In July, the government released a national climate change plan for the 2026-2030 period, targeting a 17-percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP by 2030 compared with 2025 levels. The plan also vowed to deliver the country's carbon peaking target on schedule and fulfill the 2030 nationally determined contributions. Li said China will promote green and low-carbon development in key sectors including energy, industry, transport, and urban and rural construction, accelerate the development of the national carbon market, and advance the building of a climate adaptive society. Also on Wednesday, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology released an action plan on controlling both the total amount and intensity of carbon emissions across the industrial and information technology sectors for the 2026-2030 period to speed up China's green and low-carbon transition. The plan called for improving carbon emission management in key industries, accelerating the development of zero-carbon factories, zero-carbon computing facilities and low-carbon supply chains, establishing a carbon footprint management system for industrial products, and setting up carbon accounting mechanisms. By 2030, the plan targeted the formulation and implementation of around 400 carbon footprint accounting standards for key industrial products, the establishment of roughly 500 national-level zero-carbon factories and zero-carbon computing facilities, and an over 10-percent reduction in energy consumption per unit of value-added output of major industrial enterprises.

item.title: Chinese scientists confirm Xujiayao hominins as Denisovans, revealing shared physical traits
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 23:09:00
Photo: Courtesy of Fu Qiaomei Chinese scientists have identified the Xujiayao hominins, whose fossils were unearthed in North China’s Hebei Province, as Denisovans, a distinct branch of ancient humans, through palaeoproteomic analyses and morphological comparisons, revealing shared physical traits of Denisovans, a breakthrough in resolving a long-standing debate over the classification of archaic humans in East Asia during the late Middle Pleistocene, the Global Times learned from the research team on Wednesday. The study was published in the international journal Nature on Wednesday. First identified in 2010 through DNA analysis of a finger bone discovered in Denisova Cave in Siberia, Denisovans are now known to have inhabited a wide area spanning northeastern East Asia, the Qinghai-Xizang Plateau, southwestern and southeastern China, and parts of Southeast Asia from around 300,000 to 45,000 years ago, possibly later. However, despite growing fossil and molecular evidence, scientists have struggled to establish clear morphological criteria for identifying Denisovans. Identifying shared Denisovan traits requires an ideal archaeological site with molecularly confirmed Denisovan remains, abundant human fossils, well-defined stratigraphic context and reliable dating. The Xujiayao hominins, dating to 199,000 to 138,000 years ago, have recently been classified as Homo longi, a group that includes Siberian Denisovans. Excavations at the Xujiayao site from 1976 to 1979 unearthed 20 human fossils, including cranial remains, mandibles and teeth, representing at least 16 individuals at different stages of life, making it one of the hominin sites in East Asia with the clearest stratigraphic records and richest fossil assemblages from the late Middle Pleistocene. If the Xujiayao hominins are confirmed to be Denisovans, the discovery would clarify their taxonomic status, help establish the shared morphological traits among Denisovans, and address gaps in research on Denisovans compared with Neanderthals and modern humans. To clarify this question, a joint research team led by Fu Qiaomei and Xing Song, both are researchers at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, in collaboration with researchers from Nanjing Normal University, Peking University and other institutions, conducted palaeoproteomic and morphological analyses of the Xujiayao hominin fossils. The findings have provided clear evidence that the Xujiayao hominins belong to the Denisovan lineage. Building on these findings, the team has identified key Denisovan traits in the skull, jaw and teeth, including primitive features resembling those of Homo erectus and more derived characteristics shared with later members of the genus Homo. These include a low, broad cranial vault, thick skull bones, short mastoid processes, and simplified premolar chewing surfaces. Although the Xujiayao fossils lack facial remains, evidence from comparable fossils unearthed at other sites suggests that Denisovans had low, receding foreheads, prominent brow ridges, flat faces and less pronounced jaw protrusion. Using molecularly confirmed Xujiayao fossils as a reference, the study has identified shared Denisovan traits in the skull, jaw and teeth, establishing the first morphology-based identification framework for the group in the 16 years since discovery. This finding advances Denisovans from a mysterious group identified primarily through molecular evidence to an ancient human group that can be recognized, compared and classified based on morphological characteristics, fundamentally deepening people’s understanding of the pattern of human evolution in East Asia during the Middle Pleistocene.

item.title: The Philippines should not misread the message of US warship's intrusion near Xianbin Jiao: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:59:00
The Philippines Illustration: Liu Rui/GT The US warship's early-morning "quick in, quick out" and the limited tonnage of a littoral combat ship themselves demonstrate that the priority of this performance was "risk control" rather than "deterrence effect." Any calculation that drawing in outside forces can help seize gains in the South China Sea is a serious misjudgment of the situation; any act that infringes on China's sovereignty and rights will be met with resolute countermeasures. In the early hours of Tuesday, the US littoral combat ship USS Charleston illegally intruded into the waters adjacent to Xianbin Jiao of China's Nansha Qundao without approval from the Chinese government. The People's Liberation Army (PLA) Southern Theater Command Navy dispatched forces to track and monitor the US vessel in accordance with laws and regulations. A spokesperson for the PLA Southern Theater Command Navy stated clearly that China holds indisputable sovereignty over Nansha Qundao and its adjacent waters. The US' action infringes upon China's sovereign rights and interests, jeopardizes maritime security, and is detrimental to regional peace and stability. The US side should immediately cease such activities. Xianbin Jiao lies to the east of Ren'ai Jiao. In recent years the Philippines has continuously taken infringement actions in the direction of Xianbin Jiao, hyped up the so-called "environmental issue" at Xianbin Jiao and dispatched coast guard vessels to illegally linger in its lagoon. These various moves have failed under China's countermeasures. At this moment, the US sent a littoral combat ship to intrude in the early morning. The action was carefully designed. The US warship's early-morning "quick in, quick out" and the limited tonnage of a littoral combat ship themselves demonstrate that the priority of this performance was "risk control" rather than "deterrence effect." So-called "freedom of navigation" is a false proposition in the South China Sea. The US' "freedom of navigation operations" are by no means intended to safeguard genuine freedom of navigation. Fifty percent of the world's merchant ships and one-third of maritime trade pass through the South China Sea. No matter how complex the disputes, normal international commercial navigation in the South China Sea has never been obstructed. What has truly turned "freedom of navigation" into an issue is not the passage needs of merchant ships, but the close-in disruptive actions of warships carrying specific political intentions. The United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) has still not clearly stipulated whether foreign warships enjoy the right of "innocent passage." Yet many countries require that foreign warships obtain approval or provide prior notification before entering their territorial seas. China also made relevant provisions in its 1992 Law on the Territorial Sea and the Contiguous Zone. Yet the US has not joined UNCLOS to this day, while believing that it has the "right to interpret" the Convention's concepts - this is itself a paradox. Observing the reactions of the US and the Philippines before and after the incident, one intruded and the other cheered. The US side trotted out its usual "freedom of navigation" rhetoric, while the Philippine side claimed that "the US warship did not intrude into Chinese territory." These "concerted performances" carried out in the name of fulfilling security commitments and upholding rules and order resemble a carefully choreographed parade, reflecting that the "display of allied strength" by the Philippines and the US in the South China Sea is nothing more than a publicity project staged around so-called "security issues." To some extent, such activities have become a "mobile billboard" for the US to showcase the credibility of its alliances. The audience this performance is aimed at may be other US allies and partners in the Asia-Pacific, proclaiming US military dominance in the region, but China remains an unavoidable "presence" in this performance. Anti-China forces within the Philippine military and police systems are now wantonly undermining China-Philippines relations. Behind this there is the backing and cheerleading of external forces, as well as the acquiescence and indulgence of the Philippine government. These people regard US "freedom of navigation" operations in the South China Sea as chips for gaming with China and for bargaining. But Manila needs to understand that external major powers will not bear the cost of direct conflict with China for the Philippines' adventurous actions, nor will they underwrite Manila when the situation gets out of control. They can withdraw at any time, and the Philippines will have to clean up the mess itself. Disputes in the South China Sea should be resolved through consultation among countries in the region; No external force has the right to intervene. This is a principle China has consistently upheld, and it is the only correct path for maintaining long-term peace and stability in the South China Sea. The Philippine side is advised not to misread the situation and mistake a performance for a "backer." The fact that this incident occurred in the early morning proves that any unauthorized infringement and intrusion is under China's monitoring and control. The Southern Theater Command Navy possesses all-weather situational awareness and rapid-response capabilities in the South China Sea, and is able to promptly detect, grasp, and handle relevant developments. China has indisputable sovereignty over the Nansha Qundao and their adjacent waters, and the Theater Command forces remain on high alert at all times. Manila needs to see clearly that the early-morning "quick in, quick out" performance by the US warship is not proof that "someone has its back," but rather a preview that "risks must be borne by oneself." Any calculation that drawing in outside forces can help seize gains in the South China Sea is a serious misjudgment of the situation; any act that infringes on China's sovereignty and rights will be met with resolute countermeasures.

item.title: Wider yuan use facilitates global trade
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:44:00
A landscape design of the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing, October 19, 2026 Photo: VCG Chinese and foreign officials and experts engaged in intensive discussions on the international use of the yuan at the ongoing Annual Conference of the Financial Street Forum (FSF) 2026 in Beijing on Wednesday, saying that the continuous progress in the yuan's internationalization will facilitate global trade and inject certainty into the world economy. "In recent years, China has steadfastly advanced financial reform and opening-up, playing a constructive role in global financial governance. The yuan has become the largest settlement currency for China's external receipts and payments, the world's second-largest trade finance currency, and the third-largest payment currency. Its weight in the IMF's Special Drawing Rights currency basket ranks third globally," You Jun, vice chairperson of the Standing Committee of the Beijing Municipal People's Congress, said in a speech at a sub-forum of the FSF. Looking at the current development landscape, the international use of the yuan is accelerating its shift from quantitative change to qualitative transformation, Zhang Hui, president of Bank of China, said in a speech. Cross-border yuan settlement is moving from "available" to "routinely used," cross-border yuan investment and financing are evolving from "usable" to "user-friendly," and the cross-border payment network is transitioning from "connected" to "seamlessly accessible," according to Zhang. "Yuan business is an important part of the wider UK-China financial relationship," British Ambassador to China Peter Wilson said in his speech. He said that London - the leading offshore yuan center outside Asia - will continue to give play to its own advantages and support the development of the offshore yuan market. "This year, the Bank of China has become the UK's second yuan-clearing bank. This is a really important milestone, which strengthens London's yuan infrastructure even further and gives businesses more choice in clearing and settlement," Wilson said. "China has been Indonesia's largest trading partner for more than a decade… The economic relationship is already very strong, and naturally this creates opportunities for businesses to use the Indonesian rupiah or yuan directly without using a third currency," Yulian Wihantoro, chief representative of Bank Indonesia in Beijing, said at the sub-forum "It is about making business more efficient and competitive. This is where the cooperation between Bank Indonesia and the People's Bank of China becomes very important. Our two central banks work very closely to develop a framework infrastructure for local currency transactions," Wihantoro said. "The yuan's internationalization has a stable and trustworthy foundation, which is what the development of the world economy and finance needs. Accelerating the yuan's internationalization is of profound significance for stabilizing the global economy," Xi Junyang, a professor at the Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, told the Global Times on Wednesday. Xi Junyang said that expanding trade between China and its trading partners was strengthening incentives to settle transactions in yuan. Amid rising geopolitical risks, some countries are seeking to diversify their currency use to mitigate financial risks. Settling directly in yuan can reduce transaction costs by eliminating the need for intermediate currency conversions and limit exposure to exchange-rate fluctuations associated with those conversions, the professor said.

item.title: China to improve detection of magnitude 1.0-2.5 earthquakes under 15th Five-Year Plan
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:40:00
An illustration of a user interface of earthquake warning system. Photo: VCG China will further improve its earthquake monitoring network during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-30), with the goal of enabling the country to detect earthquakes of magnitude 1.0 to 2.5 across different regions, China Central Television (CCTV) News reported on Wednesday, citing information released at a State Council Information Office press conference. According to the report, China will establish dense geophysical observation networks in key areas to monitor ground deformation, fluids and electromagnetic activity. Deep-well observation stations will also be built in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei and other regions to obtain scientific data with higher precision and greater spatial and temporal resolution, enhancing the ability to detect earthquake signals. China will also build seismic observation stations in coastal waters and densify the network of seismic monitoring stations in southwestern and northwestern regions, expanding the coverage of seismic monitoring in offshore areas and western China. Various specialized seismic networks will be integrated into the national monitoring system, CCTV News reported. Earthquake monitoring capability is a key indicator in earthquake prevention and disaster reduction. It measures the smallest-magnitude earthquake that a region's seismic network can accurately record. The lower the magnitude threshold, the greater the monitoring capability, the CCTV report explained. Earthquakes below magnitude 3 are generally difficult for people to feel unless they occur at shallow depths. The latest plan builds on China's existing earthquake monitoring and early warning infrastructure. China completed its National Earthquake Early Warning Project in July 2024, establishing a network of 15,899 observation stations across the country, according to a report from the Xinhua News Agency. At the time, authorities said the network could detect earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or above in most parts of the country, magnitude 2.0 or above in eastern regions and magnitude 1.0 or above in densely populated areas including the Beijing metropolitan area and the Yangtze River Delta. For comparison, Natural Resources Canada says its seismic network can detect all earthquakes with magnitude exceeding 3 in eastern Canada, with the detection threshold reaching magnitude 2.5 or greater in densely populated areas. In the US, the US Geological Survey (USGS) lists a detection threshold of magnitude 1.0 or greater for a seismic monitoring network near Parkfield, California. Global Times

item.title: China steps up support for commercialization of technological breakthroughs
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 22:26:00
Production line at the satellite intelligent manufacturing pilot base of Hongqing Technology Photo: IC China on Wednesday outlined guidelines to deepen the integration of technological and industrial innovation, calling for decisive breakthroughs in critical core technologies, faster commercialization of frontier technologies, a stronger role for enterprises in research and development (R&D), and greater support from long-term capital for hard technology. The guidelines aim to break down barriers between technological innovation and industrial development, shifting away from the traditional approach of considering commercialization only after research results have been produced, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Science and Technology said on Wednesday. The goal is to strengthen the integration of research and industrial applications, with enterprises playing a leading role in translating scientific advances into productive forces, the spokesperson added. The guidelines place greater emphasis on connecting scientific research with industrial demand and translating technological advances into products and economic output, Chinese economist Hu Qimu told the Global Times on Wednesday. Scientific advances can become productive forces only when applied in industrial settings and translated into products and economic output, he said. To better connect technological innovation with industrial demand, the guidelines called for reforming the organization of national research projects, with greater participation from enterprises, venture capital institutions and end users in project planning and evaluation. They also seek to facilitate the commercialization of research findings by encouraging companies to lead projects with clear industrial application goals. The guidelines identified several priority areas for technological breakthroughs, including integrated circuits, industrial machine tools, high-end instruments, advanced materials and biomanufacturing. They also call for breakthroughs in key basic software and advances in basic components, basic materials, advanced foundational processes and industrial technology foundations. Beyond breakthroughs in existing industrial technologies, the guidelines also seek to foster emerging and future industries. The guidelines also call for accelerating the development of emerging industries such as new energy, new materials and aerospace, while promoting the commercialization of frontier technologies including embodied intelligence, brain-computer interfaces and nuclear fusion energy. These developments come as China seeks to better align its growing technological capabilities with industrial demand, balancing the pursuit of breakthroughs in frontier technologies with the need to translate research findings into commercially viable applications and sustained economic growth. "China has accumulated substantial research capabilities and patent resources, yet bottlenecks persist in some industrial technologies, highlighting gaps between scientific research and industrial demand," according to Hu. "Scientific advances can become productive forces only when they are applied in industrial settings and translated into products, corporate profits and economic output," he said. The new approach seeks to remove barriers between researchers and manufacturers, allowing industrial needs to guide technological development while enabling new technologies to reshape production models, he stressed. The guidelines also seek to expand enterprises' access to research resources. They propose opening pilot programs under the National Natural Science Foundation of China to private enterprises, expanding enterprise innovation development joint funds and improving companies' access to major scientific research facilities and instruments. Large enterprises are encouraged to open research platforms, application scenarios and supply chains to smaller businesses. Patient capital is particularly important for frontier technologies that require years or even decades of sustained investment and repeated technological refinement, Hu said. Relying solely on government funding or companies' own resources may be insufficient, given businesses' need to maintain cash flow and profitability, he added. "Short-term capital cannot effectively support technological innovation that requires years of sustained effort," Hu said, adding that better matching financing horizons with research cycles would allow companies to concentrate on long-term breakthroughs while providing stronger financial support for the real economy. The move comes as China continues to increase its investment in scientific research while seeking to improve the commercial returns on innovation. China's R&D expenditure reached 3.93 trillion yuan ($588.71 billion) in 2025, up 8.2 percent year-on-year and accounting for 2.8 percent of GDP, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on October 16. Enterprises accounted for 77.4 percent of total R&D spending. Notably, despite substantial investment in R&D, challenges remain in translating research into industrial applications. In 2025, the industrialization rate of invention patents held by Chinese enterprises reached 54.0 percent, up 0.7 percentage points from 2024, according to the China National Intellectual Property Administration. The rates for universities and research institutions stood at 10.1 percent and 17.2 percent, respectively. Some industries may still need to adapt their production models to accommodate new technologies, underscoring the need for policy support to facilitate the integration of technological advances into industrial applications. Guidance for technologies developed in one sector could also find applications in another, making cross-industry collaboration and access to application scenarios important to the process, Hu said.

item.title: Global Times 'Overseas China Week' photo exhibition in Heidelberg offers closer look at China's green transition, innovation and everyday life
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:51:00
The Green and Innovation: China and Germany Embark on a Vibrant Future photo exhibition Photo: Hu Yuwei/GT Creative cultural products and multimedia reports by the Global Times on display at the exhibition Photo: Hu Yuwei/GT Guests show creative cultural products at the exhibition. Photo: Hu Yuwei/GT He also spoke about exchanges between China and Germany on technologies such as triple-glazed windows and gas-filled glazing. Chinese companies subsequently applied related technologies in production. In his view, the value of technological exchange lies not merely in introducing a product, but in translating the experience accumulated in different countries into practical applications. A guest visits the photo exhibition. Photo: Cao Siqi/GT From technological innovation to everyday life At IFA Berlin 2026, held in September, a robot developed by Shenzhen-based EngineAI interacted enthusiastically with visitors. The exhibition featured a photograph of people gathering around the robot: some were filming with their phones, while others leaned forward to observe it, creating a scene filled with curiosity about the interaction between humans and machines. A veteran German business journalist told the Global Times that robots were no longer merely technological concepts confined to laboratories. They were becoming products that appeared at exhibitions and interacted directly with the public. The journalist said the photograph gave her a sense of the "warmth" and "hope" that emerge as machines become part of human life. Similar discussions arose beside another photograph in the exhibition's second chapter "Driven by Innovation." In September 2026, an electric bus made by Chinese automaker BYD served as an official shuttle at the 72nd IAA Transportation trade fair in Hanover, Germany. For German visitors, this was hardly an unfamiliar scene. As Chinese new energy vehicles enter more overseas markets, the German public is increasingly likely to encounter Chinese electric vehicles on the road. The photograph naturally prompted discussion that extended beyond a single shuttle bus to electric mobility, the energy transition and the development of China's automotive industry. Frank Sieren, a German columnist, author and veteran journalist who has covered China for major German media outlets, told the Global Times that the photographs might surprise many Germans because their existing perceptions of China did not necessarily encompass every aspect of the country's development. He said the exhibition offered a broader perspective, allowing visitors to see what China was doing and better understand its development capabilities. He stressed that understanding a country requires looking at its different facets rather than relying on a single, one-sided impression. A photo in the exhibition: A volunteer medical team from Shanghai, organized by the Red Cross Society of China, screens local children for congenital heart disease in Kashi, Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, in May 2023. Sieren's own impressions of Chinese cities echoed the exhibition's focus on modernization. He spoke particularly warmly of Xiong'an New Area, saying he liked the way it combined modern architecture with the natural environment, creating a good balance between the two. In his view, Xiong'an's modernization was not simply about the size of the city or the height of its buildings. It addressed a question that ordinary people could readily understand: Can a city preserve natural spaces and provide a more comfortable living environment while developing rapidly? The photographs of Xiong'an in the exhibition presented China's urban development from precisely this perspective. They showed waterways, green spaces and modern buildings interwoven in the urban landscape. Since China announced plans to establish the Xiong'an New Area in April 2017, the city has evolved from a blueprint into a vibrant city. This new area is designed to relieve functions that are non-essential to Beijing's role as the national capital and advance the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. In the exhibition's third chapter "Path to Modernization," a photograph of a traditional culture class at a kindergarten in Lhasa, Southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, taken in 2023, turned visitors' attention to China's border regions. The image came from an on-the-ground reporting trip by Global Times journalist Shan Jie. It captured the sincere, radiant smiles of Tibetan children, a scene that moved visitors at the exhibition. Rather than relying on textual explanations, the photograph conveyed a picture of life in Xizang through an authentic everyday scene. It offered German audiences a glimpse of the region's development and the lives of its people, illustrating that modernization is not simply about the growth of macroeconomic indicators. It is also reflected in the smiles on people's faces and in the security, well-being and happiness that ordinary people can experience in their daily lives. Understanding begins with seeing one another For Chinese and German participants amid debates over geopolitics and international trade, the exhibition carried an additional significance. Jörg Lau, an international affairs journalist at the German weekly newspaper Die Zeit, told the Global Times that amid disagreements over issues such as market access and trade practices, it was important to focus on areas where cooperation remained possible and explore new opportunities for collaboration. The exhibition offered concrete examples that could help people "find a path toward a future characterized by greater cooperation," he said. He also advised German media colleagues to "go to China and see for themselves," describing firsthand visits as one of the most direct and effective ways to understand a country. This helps explain why the exhibition began with concrete scenes. When visitors see industries continuing beneath solar panels, green spaces preserved in modern cities, children learning traditional culture and musicians performing together on stage, China becomes more than an abstract label associated with "great-power competition," a "technology race" or a "trade rival." It becomes a place of cities, technologies and everyday jobs, inhabited by people with their own lives and genuine emotions. The value of the photo exhibition in Heidelberg lies not in leading every visitor to exactly the same conclusions, but in offering concrete images that invite people to pause, observe, ask questions and exchange views. When people from different countries recognize familiar challenges in these scenes while discovering the different ways others are addressing them, a starting point for mutual understanding begins to emerge. Jörg Lau, international correspondent for German media Die Zeit, visits the photo exhibition and tries the panda brooch. Photo: Hu Yuwei/GT

item.title: Is Elon Musk building a 'flying car' because he has been 'pushed out' of traditional auto race by China?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 21:47:00
Chinese NEVs Illustration: Liu Xiangya/GT Editor's Note: Currently, China's economy is steadily advancing along the path of high-quality development, even as domestic and international circumstances become increasingly complex. Some Western media, due to misunderstanding or bias, have repeatedly questioned or even distorted China's economic development. Accordingly, the Global Times launches the "Q&A on China's Economy" column to publish opinion pieces to present facts and clarify perceptions. Tesla recently unveiled its next-generation Roadster, which can briefly take flight and perform an aerial flip, drawing global attention. The Wall Street Journal published an article arguing that "Elon Musk's latest vision for the company's sports car has more to do with China than cold-gas rocket thrusters." It suggested that Musk "is leaving the mainstream car market to the Chinese" because "many Western automakers are unable to compete without government intervention." The article also claimed that some Western automakers are feeling the same pressure as Musk to either "move up" or "be pushed out." But does the rise of China's auto industry really mean that automakers from other countries are being forced off the track? The competitive pressure generated by China's auto industry is indeed a reality that automakers around the world cannot ignore. Musk himself has publicly described Chinese automakers as the "most competitive in the world." According to the International Energy Agency, global electric vehicle sales exceeded 20 million in 2025, with Chinese automakers accounting for around 60 percent of sales and roughly three-quarters of global EV production. At this year's Paris Motor Show, the presence of more than 20 Chinese auto brands attracted considerable attention in Europe. Chinese companies have evolved from important participants in the global auto industry into formidable competitors in an expanding range of markets and technological fields. However, interpreting Tesla's Roadster unveiling as a simple retreat from the mainstream market is misleading. From the outset, the Roadster was designed for a niche market, serving as a showcase for Tesla's technological capabilities and brand image. It is not just Tesla. In recent years, nearly all leading global automakers have placed greater emphasis on autonomous driving, connected vehicles and AI applications, reflecting a broader industry consensus on the future of mobility and automotive technology. In fact, most established automakers have not abandoned the mass market. On the contrary, they are stepping up efforts to compete for this core segment of the automotive market. Volkswagen and Renault are still developing more affordable electric vehicles and Toyota and Honda are maintaining dual-track strategies involving both hybrids and pure electric vehicles. The transformation underway in the global auto industry is therefore far more complex than a scenario in which Chinese companies take over the mass market while Western automakers retreat to the premium segment. To understand this transformation, it is essential to examine the sources of China's automotive competitiveness. Technological innovation in the auto industry has often followed a pattern in which new technologies are introduced in premium models before gradually spreading to ordinary vehicles. The more advanced the technology, the higher the price tends to be. As the technology matures and becomes more widely available, features once reserved for high-end cars eventually find their way into more affordable models. The intense competition in China's auto market is accelerating this process. In 2025, around 70 percent of the battery electric vehicles sold in China were priced below the average price of conventional gasoline cars. Smart cockpits, advanced driver-assistance systems, efficient electric drivetrains and ultra-fast charging are increasingly available in vehicles that ordinary consumers can afford. Whether Musk's "flying sports car" will ever prove practical remains to be seen. China's auto industry, however, has already demonstrated that new technologies need not be reserved for a privileged few; they can also benefit the wider public. The fundamental strength of China's auto industry lies in its ability to closely integrate technological innovation, large-scale manufacturing and market demand, enabling advanced technologies to be translated into products more quickly and made accessible to more consumers. This is underpinned by the country's long-developed industrial ecosystem. Close coordination across the power battery, electric motor, electronic controls and intelligent manufacturing sectors allows automakers to iterate technologies and develop new products more rapidly. China's vast domestic market provides a wealth of real-world application scenarios, while consumers' growing demand for intelligent and electrified vehicles continues to push companies to improve their products. Chinese automakers also face intense competition, and a number of new-energy vehicle companies have already been eliminated in recent years. Yet it is this competitive environment that has helped drive greater industrial efficiency and innovation, propelling the sector to the forefront of the global industry. Seen in this light, portraying the growth of China's auto industry as "swallowing up markets" deliberately amplifies the perceived threat of competition while overlooking the new opportunities and changes that healthy competition can create. Tesla's entry into China injected fresh competition into the domestic market, producing a "catfish effect" that spurred local manufacturers to improve. The establishment of Tesla's Shanghai Gigafactory also put pressure on Chinese automakers, but Chinese suppliers gained technical expertise and experience through production partnerships, improving both efficiency and quality. This has been a process of mutual development. Today, cooperation between Chinese and international automakers, such as Xpeng and Volkswagen, as well as Geely and Ford, further demonstrates how the global auto industry is building new networks of innovation. More than a century of automotive history has been a story of competition driving innovation and technology becoming increasingly accessible. The US once revolutionized the industry through mass production; Japanese automakers raised efficiency through lean manufacturing; and European carmakers built deep strengths in technology and branding. Today, the rise of China's auto industry is adding a new chapter to that history. Rather than treating market competition as a zero-sum game in which one side's gains must come at the other's expense, automakers should focus on strengthening their competitiveness through innovation and cooperation. China's automotive rise has not deprived the global auto industry of a future. On the contrary, it has opened up more possibilities for the industry's future.

item.title: GT Voice: Chip export boom reveals deepening China-South Korea complementarity
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-21 20:47:00
Illustration: Chen Xia/GT South Korea's exports are becoming a showcase of the global technology industry. During the first 20 days of October, South Korea's semiconductor exports surged 222.5 percent year-on-year to reach $27.5 billion, setting a new record. The chip exports accounted for 44.7 percent of the country's total, up 16.2 percentage points from a year earlier, the Yonhap News Agency reported on Wednesday. By destination, chip exports to China soared 154.4 percent to $16.6 billion, and exports to the US stood at $10.7 billion. Viewed over the longer term, this round of South Korea's export growth extends an AI-driven expansion of global computing demand that has been building for years. In 2024, South Korean chip exports rose to $141.9 billion, up 43.9 percent year-on-year. In 2025, the figure climbed to $173.4 billion, up 22.2 percent. South Korea's semiconductor exports have kept surging this year. In the first quarter, they reached $78.5 billion, up 139 percent year-on-year, and in the first half year, they hit $192.4 billion, exceeding the whole of 2025. The Bank of Korea in August raised the country's economic growth forecast this year to 3.3 percent - an increase of 0.7 percentage points and the highest level since 2021. The rationale behind this upward revision was that the extraordinary prosperity of South Korea's semiconductor sector was spreading from exports into domestic consumption, investment and other areas of local demand, steering the country's economy onto a more solid trajectory of growth. The massive jump in South Korea's exports to China stands out. At $16.6 billion, the figure far outpaces the value of shipments to the US. This export pattern reflects two things. On one hand, China's ongoing investment in AI large-language model training, data center construction and digital infrastructure is unleashing enormous demand for memory chips. On the other, Asia's regional semiconductor supply chain retains remarkable resilience despite geopolitical disturbances outside the region. The deep complementarity between the Chinese and South Korean technology industries rests on solid structural foundations. China is one of the world's largest semiconductor markets, with integrated circuit imports rising 63.5 percent year-on-year to $499 billion in the first nine months of this year. Samsung and SK Hynix together hold roughly 70 percent of the global memory chip supplies, and both companies' Chinese plants are deeply embedded in local supply chains. With the world's largest demand market on one side and irreplaceable high-end supply on the other, this deeply intertwined pattern, where each side is present in the other's industrial landscape, is not something that external factors can easily change. But challenges remain behind the eye-catching data. South Korea's chip exports are mostly concentrated in the memory sector. At the same time, the technology export controls implemented by certain countries pose potential risks too. This is precisely why both the space and necessity for deeper China-South Korea industrial chain cooperation are on the rise. If South Korea hopes to translate its current export momentum into sustainable long-term growth, relying solely on technological upgrades and product iteration will not be enough. The more important step lies in proactive industrial chain-level planning, deepening coordination with the broader Asian semiconductor ecosystem, and above all, preserving and expanding the depth of cooperation with China. This is a strategic issue that will determine whether South Korea can retain sufficient room for maneuver in an increasingly fragmented global trade environment. The 17th round of negotiations on Phase II of the China-South Korea Free Trade Agreement, held in Seoul last week, placed services and investment at the core of discussions. This suggests that the two sides may open greater room for institutional opening-up in information technology, high-end manufacturing and the digital economy, extending semiconductor complementarity currently concentrated in goods trade into other fields. Over the medium and long term, complementarity between the Chinese and South Korean industrial chains is far from reaching its ceiling. As global technology supply chains continue to face considerable uncertainty, deeper cooperation grounded in market logic and industrial reality will not only sustain South Korea's export curve, but also inject greater stability into the regional economy.
